title: Combined effects of silicon content, prior deformation and partitioning conditions on retained austenite and mechanical properties of a quenched and partitioned 0.4% C advanced high-strength steel
abstract: Quenching and Partitioning (Q&P) has become one of the established processing routes for producing advanced high-strength steels (AHSS), owing to its ability to engineer microstructures that balance high strength and ductility through retained austenite (RA) stabilization. However, the alternative Deformation–Quenching and Partitioning (DQ&P) pathway remains relatively underexplored. This study investigates the combined effects of silicon content, prior deformation, and partitioning parameters on RA stabilization and mechanical behavior in two medium-carbon steels (0.4C–2Mn–XSi–1Cr–0.02Al–0.49Ni, wt.%) with Si contents of X = 0.25 wt% (L-Si) and X = 1.5 wt% (H-Si). Three deformation passes (true strain ≈0.2/pass) were applied at 850 °C prior to quenching. Partitioning was performed at 250 °C and 300 °C for 1000 s, with additional holding times (10–10000 s) examined for selected conditions. Microstructural evolution was characterized using dilatometry, electron microscopy, and X-ray diffraction; mechanical behavior was evaluated via tensile testing. The high Si content effectively suppressed cementite precipitation and bainite formation, enabling higher RA fractions of ∼20 vol% at 300 °C and ∼17 vol% at 250 °C, with 1000 s identified as the optimal partitioning time. In the low-Si steel, ∼14 vol% RA was obtained at 250 °C after 1000 s, and 17 vol% after 10000 s. Applied deformation resulted in higher RA fractions compared to non-deformed Q&P steels. However, up to 23 vol% bainite formed in the low-Si steel at 300 °C, consuming the available austenite. Both steels exhibited pronounced TRIP behavior. The high-Si steel partitioned at 300 °C (1000 s) achieved an excellent strength–ductility balance (1822 MPa and 9.3% elongation), while the low-Si steel partitioned at 250 °C also demonstrated competitive performance, highlighting the positive role of deformation.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Advanced high-strength steels (AHSSs) have garnered significant attention in the automotive industry owing to their exceptional balance between strength and ductility, commonly expressed through the strength–elongation product [ 1 ]. Typically, modern AHSS consists of complex microstructures, for instance, a mixture of hard, load-bearing martensite and/or bainite complemented by metastable austenite and fine dispersion of carbides. The metastable austenite may also transform to martensite under applied stress or strain, enabling sustained work-hardening via the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect and delaying the onset of plastic instability [ 2–4 ]. Within this framework, the quenching and partitioning (Q&P) process has emerged as a well-established heat treatment for developing martensite–retained austenite (RA) microstructures. In Q&P steels, RA is deliberately carbon-enriched and thereby stabilized at room temperature. The common Q&P cycle involves interrupted quenching of fully austenitized steel to the quench stop temperature (T q ) between the martensite start (M s ) and finish (M f ) temperatures to form a controlled fraction of primary martensite (PM). Subsequent isothermal holding at the partitioning temperature (T p ) near the T q  facilitates carbon partitioning from supersaturated martensite into the remaining austenite. This carbon enrichment suppresses further transformation of austenite to secondary martensite (SM) during final cooling, enabling tailored fractions, morphologies, and stabilities of RA [ 5 , 6 ].

Realizing the full potential of Q&P steels requires precise control over three interdependent factors: (i) the chemical driving forces for austenite stabilization (notably carbon (C)), (ii) the morphology and length scale of martensite/austenite interfaces that govern partitioning kinetics and mechanical constraint, and (iii) the suppression of competing reactions – such as cementite precipitation in martensite and bainitic transformation of austenite – that consume available C and reduce the enrichment of RA [ 7–9 ]. In this regard, Si can play a pivotal role in Q&P steel chemistry due to its negligible solubility in cementite, making it a potent suppressor of cementite formation during partitioning [ 9–11 ]. This preserves carbon for further austenite enrichment and stabilizes higher RA fractions at room temperature [ 10 , 12 , 13 ]. Si also retards the kinetics of bainitic transformation in carbon steels during isothermal heat treatment. Extensive studies suggest that around 1.5 wt% Si is an effective threshold in low- and medium-carbon Q&P grades [ 9 , 14 ]. Below this level, austenite tends to decompose into bainite and/or martensite during partitioning or final quenching, resulting in reduced RA fractions and diminished TRIP effects [ 15 , 16 ]. However, very high Si content poses industrial challenges, including the formation of adherent fayalite (Fe 2 SiO 4 ) scale during hot processing and galvanizing issues, prompting efforts to reduce its content without compromising RA stability and ductility [ 17 ].

In addition, during Q&P processing, transition carbides or cementite (θ) precipitation and bainite formation often overlap with carbon partitioning, even in high-Si steels, complicating the stabilization of RA and introducing spatial heterogeneity in the stability. Microstructural studies have revealed that transition carbides can form within martensite before or during partitioning, and their slow dissolution can throttle carbon release to austenite. Additionally, Mn and C segregation can locally alter M s  and transformation pathways, producing banded distributions of martensite, bainite, and RA [ 7 , 18 ]. These interactions are now recognized as defining features of Q&P processing maps, especially at low partitioning temperatures (200–300 °C) that are relevant to the present study.

Beyond chemistry, prior austenite grain size (PAGS) and its control via thermomechanical processing can influence Q&P microstructure evolution. PAGS affects M s  and the kinetics of martensite transformation through its impact on nucleation site density and the strength of austenite. Grain refinement typically lowers M s  and increases early-stage nucleation density, while restricting interface mobility during later stages, altering the balance between PM, RA retention and stability, and subsequent transformations. Fine austenite grains also increase the interface area available for C transfer and influence diffusion distances and local constraints, thereby shaping RA morphology and stability [ 19–22 ]Refined PAGS and, in consequence, the lath martensite packet size in 0.3C–4.0Mn–1.6Si–1.0Cr (chemical compositions are in wt.% hereafter) steel were reported to achieve a clear plasticity enhancement due to activated deformation twinning and strain-induced martensitic transformation [ 23 ].

A direct deformation-quenching and partitioning (DQ&P) process has been proposed by Somani et al. [ 24 ]. If the strain and temperature are sufficiently high, deformation can induce dynamic or static recrystallization, leading to PAGS refinement and/or an increase in the dislocation density of the refined martensite that accelerates carbon transport into austenite and modifies plastic constraint and martensite lath morphology. Peng et al. [ 25 ] showed that 60% compression at 870 °C prior to Q&P refined martensite laths and elevated dislocation density in both martensite and austenite, leading to improved strength and modest ductility gains. Ghosh et al. [ 26 ] combined multi-pass thermomechanical control rolling with Q&P and achieved ∼12 vol% RA and ultra-high tensile strength (2.1–2.3 GPa) in 0.4C–2Mn–(0.25, 0.75, 1.5) Si steels, after partitioning for 1000 s at 200 °C, underscoring the potential of deformation-enhanced Q&P routes. However, the mechanical properties were evaluated only at a low partitioning temperature (200 °C) and a single partitioning time (1000 s). As a result, it remains unclear whether the benefits of deformation-assisted RA stabilization can be preserved at higher partitioning time or obtained in shorter times, where bainite formation competes strongly at 250–300 °C. Therefore, the present work explicitly compares low-Si (0.25 wt%) and high-Si (1.5 wt%) variants of the same medium-carbon steel subjected to DQ&P schedules to elucidate the coupled effects of Si content, deformation, partitioning time, and temperature on the thermal and mechanical stability of RA as well as on subsequent tensile properties. The microstructural data of Miettunen et al. [ 8 ] for the same steel processed by conventional Q&P without prior deformation enables the comparison to reveal the influence of deformation on RA fraction and stability controlled by the carbon partitioning. A particularly compelling research question was whether deformation-induced stabilization of RA can compensate for reduced Si content, offering an alternative pathway to achieve optimized strength–ductility combinations. Dilatometry and detailed microstructural characterization by various electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction (XRD) were employed to quantitatively assess phase transformations and RA characteristics.

sections.heading: Materials and experimental procedures
paragraphs:
The medium-carbon, low alloy steels used in the present study were specifically designed as potential candidates for Q&P AHSS [ 8 ]. The steels were produced by vacuum induction melting, cast into ingots, and hot rolled to 3 mm-thick plates. The chemical compositions are given in  Table 1 
                      . The alloys differ only in their Si content: a high-Si (H-Si) grade (1.5 wt% Si) and a low-Si (L-Si) grade (0.25 wt% Si).

The DQ&P processing was performed using a Gleeble 3800 thermomechanical simulator. The cylindrical specimens (6 mm in diameter, 9 mm in length) were extracted from the mid-thickness region of a rolled plate, with their longitudinal axis aligned parallel to the rolling direction. Dilatometric data as well as time-temperature profiles were recorded during the entire process. The cycle included full austenitization at 1150 °C for 120 s, followed by cooling at 5 °C/s to 850 °C, holding for 10 s, and hot deformation in three compression passes (true strain ∼0.2/pass) at a strain rate of 1 s −1  with 25 s inter-pass holding and holding time before the start of quenching. After deformation, samples were quenched by helium gas to 150 °C to form ∼75 vol% PM and ∼25 vol% untransformed austenite, as determined by dilatometry results. The schematic overview of the applied process is presented in  Fig. 1 
                      . The main partitioning treatments were conducted at 250 °C and 300 °C for 1000 s.

To examine the influence of a wider range of partitioning times at optimum partitioning temperatures on the fraction of RA and the kinetics of carbon partitioning and other possible isothermal phase transformations, additional samples were subjected to isothermal holding for 10, 100, 1000, and 10000 s at 250 °C (L-Si) and 300 °C (H-Si). These temperatures were chosen, according to the initial results, to provide suitable conditions for carbon diffusion from martensite into austenite while minimizing excessive bainitic transformation for each Si level. Following partitioning, all specimens were cooled to room temperature at a rate of 30 °C/s.

Since the Gleeble cylindrical specimens were necessarily short due to the high compressive strain, it was not possible to use them for standard (sub)size tensile tests. Therefore, identical thermomechanical processing routes were replicated on a pilot-scale thermomechanical rolling line at the University of Oulu, and plates were used for extracting the specimens for evaluating the tensile properties of DQ&P treatments. Details of the preparation of materials for tensile samples by thermomechanical rolling have been described in Ref. [ 26 ].

The mechanical properties of the steels were evaluated through uniaxial tensile testing. Flat tensile specimens (gauge length 25 mm, width 6 mm, thickness 2 mm) were machined along the rolling direction. Tests were performed on a Zwick Z100 universal testing machine at a nominal strain rate of 10 −3  s −1 , in accordance with ASTM  E8 /E8M. Yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS), uniform elongation (UE), and total elongation (TE) were determined from the mean value of at least three specimens per condition.

Microstructural characterization was performed using a combination of complementary techniques. A laser scanning confocal microscope (Keyence VK-X200) was employed to reveal the prior austenite grain structure through picric acid and thermal etching methods. Detailed microstructural observations were carried out using a field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, JEOL JSM-7900F) operating at 18 kV. A field-emission scanning electron microscope equipped with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was employed to examine the morphology and crystallographic orientation of RA with step sizes ranging from 40 to 70 nm. The EBSD data were processed using AZtec Crystal software. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) JEOL 2200FS EFTEM/STEM operated at 200 kV on thin foils prepared by twin-jet electropolishing was used to investigate the retained austenite and martensite, as well as carbide precipitation behavior. XRD analyses were performed using Rigaku SmartLab X-Ray  diffractometer  (9 kW), with a Co-Kα source, scanned over a 2θ range of 30–135°, to determine the RA volume fraction and C concentration. Quantitative phase analysis was achieved through Rietveld refinement in accordance with ASTM  E975 , and  the  lattice parameter of RA obtained from XRD was used to estimate its average C content based on the empirical relation [ 22 ], described in Equation  (1) :

sections.heading: Effect of deformation on prior austenite grain size and M s  temperature
paragraphs:
The prior austenite grain structure and size as a result of hot deformation prior to quenching for the H-Si and L-Si steels are shown in  Fig. 2 
                         . After the deformation process, the average value of the PAGS was about 25 and 19 μm for the L-Si and H-Si steel, respectively, whereas without the prior deformation, it was about 94 and 84 μm, respectively. The comparison of PAGS with and without the deformation is presented in the  Supplementary material S1 . Although the deformation was applied at a relatively low temperature range of hot deformation (850 °C), where dynamic recovery is generally dominant, the flow-stress curves indicated that significant inter-pass softening occurred, consistent with the occurrence of static recrystallization during the short (25 s) inter-pass holding times. This ultimately enabled the formation of a substantially refined austenite structure that transformed into a finer martensite/retained-austenite morphology upon quenching. Since our primary aim was to explore the effect of prior deformation and resulting grain refinement on the Q&P process, rather than the refinement mechanism itself, a more detailed discussion of the flow-stress analysis and recrystallization kinetics is provided in the  Supplementary material S1 .

In this regard, Matsuoka et al. [ 27 ] examined the effect of grain size on athermal martensitic transformation in a metastable austenitic stainless steel (Fe–16Cr–10Ni) with grain sizes between 1 and 80 μm. They found that a PAGS above ∼20 μm has minimal effect on austenite's thermal stability, whereas refining grains below 20 μm markedly increases stability. In our context, finer grains would be expected to lower the M s  temperature, as finer grains result in more numerous grain boundaries, which slow down the martensitic transformation process overall by acting as a barrier to the movement of the martensitic transformation interface. However, grain size has less of an impact on M s  temperature than chemical composition does, according to Zhu et al. [ 28 ]. Since smaller grains increase the material resistance to the plastic deformation necessary for the martensite transformation, it is generally expected that finer grains will result in a lower M s  temperature. Equation  (2) , which is derived from Ref. [ 29 ], accounts for the delaying effects of both Si alloying and PAGS. 
                            
                               Eq. (2) 
                               M s  (°C) = 565 – 27x Mn  - 7x Si  + 10x Al  - 16x Cr  – 600 (1- exp(-0.96x C )) - 90(D PAGS ) −1/3 
                               
                            
                         where D PAGS  (μm) is the prior austenite grain size, and x Mn , x Si , x Al,  x Cr,  and x C  are the concentrations of Mn, Si, Al, Cr, and C in wt.%.  Fig. 3 
                          compares the calculated M s  as a function of D PAGS  for the H-Si and L-Si steels with the corresponding experimental values. More details on measuring the M s  temperature using dilatometry data can be found in  Supplementary material S2 .

Fig. 3  presents the variation of the M s  temperature as a function of the prior austenite grain size (D PAGS ) for both steels. The dashed curves correspond to M s  values calculated using Eq.  (2) , while the horizontal dotted lines indicate the experimentally measured M s  obtained by dilatometry (280 °C for L-Si and 264 °C for H-Si). For both compositions, Eq.  (2)  predicts a clear increase in M s  with increasing prior austenite grain size.

When the average grain size (25 μm for L-Si and 18 μm for H-Si) is used in Eq.  (2) , the calculated M s  values significantly underestimate the experimental dilatometric Ms. The deviation is approximately 8–10 °C for both steels. In contrast, when the largest measured grain size is employed (48 μm for L-Si and 35 μm for H-Si), the predicted M s  values are in very good agreement with the dilatometry results, with only marginal differences (≤2–3 °C). This behavior is physically expected. The M s  temperature determined by dilatometry corresponds to the onset of the first detectable martensitic transformation event in the bulk sample. Martensite nucleation preferentially occurs in the most unstable austenite regions, which are typically the coarsest grains due to their lower grain boundary constraint and reduced mechanical stabilization. Therefore, the experimentally measured M s  is governed by the largest (or least stable) austenite grains rather than the statistical average grain size. In overall, the L-Si steel exhibits a slightly higher M s  than the H-Si counterpart due to its coarse PAGS and the lower Si content. In practice, this means that after quenching to 150 °C, the L-Si steel has a slightly lower austenite content compared to that in the H-Si steel. This difference persists over the partitioning and is reflected in the room temperature values of the RA fraction.

Furthermore, electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) shows (presented in Supplementary material section S3) the existence of C–Mn segregation banding with local enrichment of alloying elements. Such compositional variations may locally affect the M s  temperature. However, M s  temperature obtained from dilatometry results based on the relative change in specimen diameter, reflects the bulk transformation response, inherently accounting the influence of the observed segregation bands.

sections.heading: Phase analysis during the DQ&P process
Dilatometry
paragraphs:
A high-resolution dilatometer integrated in the Gleeble simulator was used to continuously monitor the phase transformations throughout the DQ&P process at each stage of the applied processing route.  Fig. 4 
                             depicts an example of the dilatometry results (relative change in the diameter of a cylindrical specimen) for the H-Si steel at a partitioning temperature of 250 °C. As demonstrated in  Fig. 4 , the main microstructural changes and phase transformations during the process, excluding the heating part, are categorized into four different regions: Region I corresponds to the cooling of the sample after deformation at 850 °C. A pronounced volumetric expansion, associated with the formation of athermal martensite, is observed during cooling to 150 °C due to martensite formation. The PM fraction was recalculated based on the experimental dilatometry results, and this value was adopted as the representative athermal martensite volume fraction ( Table 2 
                            ), and the other phase fractions were calculated using the same methodology employed in the earlier studies [ 8 ]. However, it should be noted that all calculation methods carry an approximate uncertainty of about  
                               
                                  ± 
                               
                             5%, and this must be taken into account when interpreting the results [ 8 ]. The ±5% uncertainty applies to the phase fractions determined from dilatometry, whereas the retained austenite fraction obtained by XRD is evaluated independently with higher quantitative accuracy.

In Region II, the specimens were reheated to the partitioning temperature .  Region III represents the partitioning stage, and Region IV corresponds to the final quenching step to room temperature. Since all samples underwent identical processing up to Region III, only regions III and IV are discussed in detail in the following sections, as differences among the specimens originate from this point onward.

Figs. 5 and 6 
                            
                             compare the dilatometric behavior of the present DQ&P steels. The corresponding dilatation curves revealed three distinct stages during isothermal holding at Tp (Region III), as discussed below: 
                               
                                  Stage I: A slight initial expansion at the start of partitioning can be attributed to carbon partitioning from supersaturated martensite to austenite, which increases the lattice parameter of austenite [ 30 ]. 
                               
                               
                                  Stage II: A more pronounced expansion following Stage I, attributed mainly to isothermal transformation phenomena. According to Ref. [ 31 ], this behavior reflects the volume increase associated with the bainite reaction with simultaneous carbon partition from supersaturated martensite into the surrounding austenite. Nevertheless, the dilatometric signal alone cannot unambiguously distinguish this transformation from other concurrent phenomena. The formation of isothermal martensite, relaxation of martensite tetragonality, or simultaneous bainitic transformation may also contribute to the overall expansion, complicating the interpretation of the thermal response [ 32 , 33 ]. 
                               
                               
                                  Stage III :  According to the literature [ 26 ], in this stage sample contracts due to extensive tempering of martensite and cementite formation.

Comparing the differences emerge between the H-Si and L-Si steels, as  Fig. 5 (a) shows, the H-Si steel exhibits only the gradual expansion of Stage I that is attributed to C partitioning, with no clear indication of Stage II, i.e., isothermal transformation at T p  of 300 °C and 250 °C. In contrast,  Fig. 6 (a) demonstrates that the L-Si steel displays a pronounced Stage II expansion, particularly when partitioned at 300 °C. The onset of accelerated expansion observed after approximately 100 s likely corresponds to the onset of bainitic transformation during isothermal holding, as can be seen in  Fig. 6 (a). Toward the end of the 1000 s holding period at 300 °C, a subtle secondary increase in expansion following an extended plateau suggests progressively decreasing rate of the bainitic transformation, presumably reflecting the gradual C enrichment and stabilization of austenite. However, at the lower T p  of 250 °C, similarly to the H-Si steel, the dilatation changes are limited to a mild initial increase in Stage I due to carbon redistribution from supersaturated martensite to austenite, with negligible bainite formation.

A high Si content is known to effectively suppress carbide precipitation in Q&P steels at higher Tp values, whereas transition carbides (ε/η-carbides) can nucleate at around 250 °C [ 7 , 11 , 34 ]. Thus, the absence of rapid expansion at 250 °C suggests that if any such carbides or transformations are present, they are too limited to produce a detectable expansion in Stage II at 250 °C.

Consistent with the above considerations, two partitioning temperatures were selected for extended holding up to 10000 s to allow further time for carbon enrichment and RA stabilization: 250 °C for the L-Si steel and 300 °C for the H-Si steel.  Fig. 5 (c) shows thermal expansion in the final stage due to secondary martensite (SM) formation during the final quench. The amount of SM decreases with increasing partitioning time.  Fig. 5 (d) shows no measurable expansion up to 1000 s, indicating the absence of bainite formation even after 10000 s of partitioning, but a slight diameter reduction is observed in Stage III. This indicates that, beyond 1000 s, the maximum stabilization of austenite by carbon enrichment has been achieved at this temperature, although not all RA remains stable to room temperature (see the RA fractions after tensile test later in  Table 3 
                            ). However, the longest partitioning time leads to a reduction in strength because of martensite tempering, and therefore, 1000 s can be regarded as the most suitable duration at 300 °C for the H-Si steel.

A similar trend was observed for the L-Si steel ( Fig. 6 (d)), although SM persisted up to 1000 s, whereas after 10000 s, no SM transformation occurred. At the longest holding times (>2000 s), the dilatation curve of the L-Si steel at 250 °C shows a slow expansion ( Fig. 6 (d)), which corresponds to bainite formation. Da Silva et al. [ 31 ] have reported that bainitic transformation can occur during isothermal holding even below M s  temperature. Similarly, in the L-Si steel, the objective was to increase the fraction of RA while avoiding bainite formation; therefore, even a holding time of 1000 s was insufficient to achieve the maximum fraction of RA.

sections.heading: Final phase fraction and carbon content of retained austenite
paragraphs:
The final phase fractions were derived from dilatometry curves and XRD data, allowing a quantitative assessment of the PM formed during interrupted quenching at 150 °C and the SM developed during final cooling. The RA fractions at room temperature were quantified by XRD peak intensities, which remain sufficient for comparative analysis despite reduced precision at lower fractions below ∼5 vol%, owing to the weak and broadened diffraction peaks of the {200}γ and {220}γ reflections. The fractions of PM, RA, and SM were determined directly from XRD and dilatometric data, and the bainite phase fraction was determined by difference from RA, PM, and SM, and for L-Si steel after partitioning at 300 °C for 1000 s, the result was independently validated by EBSD-IQ deconvolution ( Supplementary Material S5 ). Good agreement was observed between the two techniques, with a bainite volume fraction of approximately 25%, as shown in  Supplementary Material S5 . The formation of isothermal martensite during holding was negligible under these conditions, consistent with prior work by An et al. [ 35 ], who demonstrated that bainitic transformation can be semi-quantitatively inferred from slope changes in dilatation curves, though a more rigorous deconvolution would require in-situ diffraction techniques. The final phase fractions are summarized in  Table 2 . A more details information on how SM analyzed is presented in the  Supplementary material S4 
                            .

For clarifying the effects of deformation, the final RA fractions obtained after the present DQ&P and previous Q&P processing [ 8 ] at different partitioning temperatures and different Si contents are illustrated in  Fig. 7 
                            (a). It can be noticed that the DQ&P process provided higher RA fractions in both the steels. The H-Si steel retained ∼20 vol% RA at 300 °C (1000 s) compared to ∼18 vol% in the non-deformed and the DQ&P L-Si retained ∼17% at 250 °C compared with ∼15 vol% without deformation. This clearly highlights the beneficial effect of deformation-induced grain size refinement on promoting austenite retention.

Fig. 7 (b) depicts the room-temperature RA fractions of the H-Si and L-Si steels after various partitioning times, indicating that the amount of stabilized RA increases with longer holding times. Obviously, this is connected with improved austenite stability with prolonged partitioning time. At T p  of 300 °C, the maximum (≈20 vol%) appears to be reached after 1000 s, whereas at 250 °C, the RA fraction is still increasing after 1000 s. The fraction of austenite at the beginning of partitioning was 25 vol% ( Table 2 ), so that all of that did not become stabilized in the experiments carried out. Furthermore, it can be seen that the higher Si content resulted in 17 vol% RA at T p  of 250 °C for 1000 s, compared to 14 vol% RA in the L-Si steel.

Fig. 8 
                             presents a section of the TTT diagram (martensite formation is excluded for the better presentation of the bainitic region) illustrating the onset of bainite formation across different temperatures and times for varying carbon concentrations, as calculated using JMatPro software. In the H-Si steel (0.4 wt% C), bainitic transformation initiates after approximately 300 s at 300 °C and 200 s at 250 °C. During the partitioning process, enrichment of carbon in the retained austenite progressively delays in the initiation of bainitic transformation, as shown in  Fig. 8 (a). Consequently, bainite does not form in the H-Si steel at partitioning temperatures of 250 °C and 300 °C. This behavior is consistent with the experimental observations. Therefore, in this case, the process route should focus on reducing the amount of SM formed. So based on  Table 2 , after partitioning at 250 °C for any time, only a small amount of SM (∼8 vol%) was formed during final quenching. When partitioned at 300 °C, the specimen exhibited approximately 7 vol% RA after 10 s and 100 s of holdings. With prolonged holding, the SM fraction progressively decreased, whereas the RA fraction increased steadily, reaching a maximum of about 20 vol% after 1000 s. Beyond this duration, further holding did not lead to more significant changes, indicating that austenite stabilization was essentially complete.

In contrast, for the L-Si steel,  Fig. 8 (b) suggests that bainite formation at 300 °C starts after about 100 s, consistent with the experimental observations ( Fig. 6 (a)), such that almost all austenite transformed to bainite before final cooling, resulting in the absence of SM and leaving only a negligible fraction of RA (<1 vol%). This confirms that, for the low Si composition, 300 °C is not a feasible partitioning temperature for this composition. At the lower partitioning temperature of 250 °C, 7.0 vol% RA was detected after 10 s of holding time. With increasing holding time up to 10000 s, the RA fraction gradually increased up to about 17 vol%. However, at these extended durations, bainite formation became evident, indicating that carbon partitioning and bainitic transformation occur concurrently during long isothermal treatments.

From a mechanistic standpoint, the contrasting phase evolution between the H-Si and L-Si steels can be attributed to the role of Si in suppressing carbide precipitation and delaying bainite formation. Consequently, carbon remains in solid solution and preferentially partitions from martensite into austenite during isothermal holding, enriching and stabilizing the austenite phase. Collectively, these results confirm that partitioning temperature, holding time, and Si concentration simultaneously govern microstructural evolution during quenching and partitioning. Higher Si levels thermodynamically inhibit carbide formation, expand the time window for carbon redistribution, and promote greater austenite stability, whereas lower Si contents exhibit accelerated bainitic transformation and a limited amount of RA at room temperature.

Estimated C contents of the RA were determined from the lattice parameter of austenite obtained by XRD (Equation  (1) ), and the results are summarized in  Table 2 . The fitting uncertainty of the austenite lattice parameter was low (±0.0002 nm), corresponding to an error in the calculated carbon content of less than ±0.02 wt%. The results reveal distinct variation in the C content depending on the Si content, partitioning temperature, and holding duration. In the H-Si steel, partitioning at 250 °C for 1000 s provided an average C content of 0.60 wt%. Partitioning at 300 °C led to a marked increment of the C content from 0.64 to 0.77 wt% within holding time from 10 to 1000 s, and still up to 0.95 wt% in holding until 10000 s. This confirms that carbon diffusion from martensite into austenite continued even up to 10000 s, progressively enriching the austenite. This is seen in the increased RA fraction from 13 to 20 vol% stabilized to room temperature ( Fig. 7 (b)). However, still some SM was present in the final structure, though in decreasing amount from 11.5 to 5 vol%, indicating that all existing austenite (≈24–25 vol% before partitioning) could not be stabilized (the M s  temperature of the SM formation during the final cooling is 95 °C according to  Table 2 , obtained from dilatometric curves). In the L-Si steel at 250 °C, carbon enrichment from 0.64 to 0.78 wt% was observed during holding from 10 to 1000 s and further up to 0.94 wt% within 10000 s. During this period, the RA fraction increased progressively from ∼7 vol% to 14 vol% within1000 s and even up to 17% after 10000 s ( Fig. 7 (b)).

Concluding from the above observations, the DQ&P process results in higher RA fractions than Q&P does. However, the effect of deformation on the carbon enrichment remains indistinct, though an enhanced diffusion rate of carbon might be expected if austenite contains more defects. However, as mentioned, static recrystallization occurred, which reduced the dislocation density, and only the grain boundary length is higher in a finer-grained structure. Higher RA stability without higher carbon content could be a result of its finer grain size, as retained from refined PAGS. The effect of PAGS was indicated by Equation  (2)  and discussed in Section  3.1 .

sections.heading: Scanning electron micrographs
paragraphs:
Figs. 9 and 10 
                            
                             show representative microstructures of the H-Si steel after partitioning at 250 °C and 300 °C, respectively, while  Figs. 11 and 12 
                            
                             correspond to the L-Si steel after partitioning at the same temperatures. As shown in  Fig. 9 (a and b), the microstructure of the H-Si steel after partitioning at 250 °C contains mainly lath martensite and martensite-austenite (M/A) constituents with inter-lath RA. Only film-like RA is retained at room temperature, whereas coarse, blocky austenite grains present during partitioning transform into SM upon final cooling.  Fig. 9 (c and d) confirm that the RA at 250 °C is mainly in the form of thin films along martensite lath boundaries (∼170–220 nm in thickness). According to  Table 2 , XRD measurements indicated that ∼17% RA remained, and the austenite of ∼8 vol% transformed to SM  Fig. 10 (a) shows the H-Si steel at a partitioning temperature of 300 °C, and  Fig. 10 (b–e) present higher-magnification images of selected areas revealing microstructural features more clearly. After partitioning at 300 °C, the H-Si steel retained a higher fraction of austenite (∼20 vol% by XRD) and, importantly, this included some blocky austenite grains.  Fig. 10 (b–e) reveal blocky RA regions averaging around 860 nm in size alongside fine films (∼130 nm). In contrast to the condition at 250 °C, the higher partitioning temperature allowed even relatively coarse austenite regions to acquire enough carbon to remain stable on cooling.

In summary, the H-Si steel exhibits predominantly film-like RA after 250 °C partitioning, but a mixture of blocky (∼0.86 μm) and film-like (∼0.13 μm) RA after 300 °C partitioning. This is in contrast to the L-Si steel.  Fig. 11  shows the microstructure of the L-Si steel partitioned at 250 °C. In comparison to the H-Si steel, the low-Si alloy reveals a noticeably higher amount of carbide precipitates in the martensite, due to the lower Si content. Partitioning has produced a very refined microstructure with RA in the form of films along martensite lath boundaries. These films (∼115–240 nm) are similar in size to those in the H-Si steel; however, any blocky austenite was not stabilized but transformed to SM upon final cooling. Thus, the L-Si steel at 250 °C retained a smaller fraction of RA (∼14 vol%,  Table 2 ) than the high-Si steel did, and that RA is confined to finely dispersed films.

Fig. 12  depicts the L-Si steel after partitioning at 300 °C. The microstructure is dominated by bainite and tempered martensite, with very little RA. In fact, dilatometry already indicated ∼23% bainitic transformation in this condition. Consistently, the SEM images ( Fig. 12 (b–d)) show numerous coarse carbides within the martensite laths, signifying cementite formation, which was later confirmed by TEM. The presence of extensive cementite and bainite confirms that much of the austenite decomposed during the 300 °C hold, leaving less than 5 vol% RA (nearly nondetectable by XRD in  Table 2 ).

sections.heading: EBSD phase analysis of microstructures
paragraphs:
EBSD mapping was performed on the samples for further morphological investigation of RA, as well as regions transformed to the SM during final cooling. In the presented results, the colored regions correspond to RA (FCC phase), while the grayscale regions represent the martensitic/bainitic constituents (BCC phase). Due to the spatial resolution limitation of EBSD for very thin RA films, the quantitative RA fraction was determined by XRD, while EBSD was used mainly for microstructural and morphological analysis. In the H-Si steel partitioned at 300 °C ( Fig. 13 
                            (a)), EBSD reveals that detected RA mainly exhibits a blocky morphology which is mostly located along prior austenite grain boundaries and inter-lath regions. These RA regions correspond to the carbon-enriched zones stabilized during partitioning, as discussed earlier.  Fig. 13 (b) (H-Si 300 °C, higher magnification) distinguishes PM from SM: the untempered SM formed during final cooling appears as very dark areas (higher defect density), whereas the tempered PM laths are relatively brighter. Conversely, as shown in  Fig. 13 (c and d), the same steel partitioned at 250 °C contains a higher proportion of fine, film-like austenite dispersed between martensitic laths. However, the limited spatial resolution of EBSD (∼80 nm) constrains the accurate quantification and indexing of these nanoscale films, and the true RA fraction is likely underestimated. Nevertheless, qualitatively, it is evident that at 250 °C, more austenite transformed to martensite (more dark regions), consistent with our earlier point that blocky RA was not retained at this lower partitioning temperature.

The L-Si steel exhibited a markedly lower fraction of RA under both partitioning conditions ( Fig. 14 
                            (a and b)). Only very small, scattered and isolated RA regions were detected (colored specks), confirming that low Si failed to stabilize much austenite. Instead, the microstructure is almost entirely BCC (martensite + bainite). Although EBSD cannot explicitly differentiate bainite from martensite (both are BCC), differences in band contrast provide useful indications. Martensite, having a high dislocation density, tends to appear darker (lower image quality), whereas bainite or well-tempered martensite appears brighter. Thus, dark gray regions likely correspond to untempered SM, while the lighter gray matrix represents a mix of bainite and tempered primary martensite. However, a precise distinction between bainitic and tempered martensitic areas is not critical to the present analysis, since both are BCC products that do not contribute to TRIP and they can be assumed to have a similar impact on the overall tensile behavior of samples.

It should also be remarked that, as most of the conditions resulted in very little detectable RA after partitioning (and even less after straining) via EBSD, meaningful post-tensile EBSD analysis of RA was only possible for the H-Si steel partitioned at 300 °C, which contained the highest RA fraction and coarser RA morphology. Therefore, we focus our post-deformation examination on that case (see Section  3.4.2 ).

sections.heading: Transmission electron microscopy
paragraphs:
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was employed to examine the morphology and crystallography of the constituent phases in selected DQ&P specimens, with particular emphasis on identifying RA, martensite variants, and carbide precipitates. Both bright-field and dark-field imaging modes were used, complemented by selected area electron diffraction (SAED) analyses recorded from regions of interest to confirm phase identity.  Fig. 15 
                             presents TEM micrographs of the H-Si and L-Si steels partitioned at 300 °C.

In the H-Si steel, a fine, dislocation-rich lath martensitic structure was observed, containing thin interlath films of RA ( Fig. 15 (a and b)). The corresponding SAED pattern acquired along the [110] zone axis ( Fig. 15 (c)) confirmed the FCC austenitic phase. Blocky RA was not detected by TEM, although its presence was confirmed by EBSD observations. Importantly, no evidence of cementite precipitation was detected in the H-Si steel despite its nominal carbon content of 0.4 wt%, indicating that the elevated Si concentration effectively suppressed carbide nucleation during partitioning.

In contrast, the L-Si steel exhibited a markedly different microstructure, characterized by frequent cementite precipitates decorating the martensitic laths ( Fig. 15 (d and e)). The diffraction pattern in  Fig. 15 (f) confirmed the orthorhombic structure of cementite (Fe 3 C), consistent with its identification by morphology and lattice spacing [ 25 , 26 , 36 ]. Consistently, Miettunen et al. [ 8 ] observed cementite precipitation in the L-Si steel during Q&P processing, but its absence in H-Si steel in Q&P processing. The η-carbide was not detected in the L-Si steel after partitioning at 300 °C.

Fig. 16 
                             depicts representative TEM bright-field ( Fig. 16 (a,d)) and dark-field ( Fig. 16 (b–e)) images of both alloys after partitioning at 250 °C. The DF images clearly reveal the presence of nanoscale RA films embedded within the martensitic matrix in both steels. The BF micrographs ( Fig. 16 (a–d)) show the presence of twinned martensite laths, suggesting the formation of SM upon final quenching from metastable RA that was insufficiently enriched in carbon. In the L-Si steel, additional fine-scale carbide precipitation was observed within the martensitic laths ( Fig. 16 (c–f)). The corresponding SAED patterns confirmed the presence of η-carbide (Fe 2 C), characterized by distinct superlattice reflections along the [011] zone. Qualitatively, the density of η-carbide precipitates decreased with increasing Si content, but even the high Si level could not fully suppress the formation of transition carbides under prolonged partitioning at low temperature. Consistently, Ghosh et al. [ 18 ] observed η-carbide precipitates even after partitioning at 200 °C despite the Si content.

The observations collectively demonstrate that the role of Si in the DQ&P microstructure is primarily both kinetic and thermodynamic. Silicon markedly inhibits cementite formation by increasing the free energy of the α/θ (ferrite/cementite) reaction, thereby retarding carbide nucleation and growth. However, its influence on transition carbide precipitation, such as η-carbide, is considerably weaker, as these metastable carbides form prior to cementite during the early stages of martensite tempering. Consequently, high Si content promotes carbon partitioning from supersaturated martensite to austenite, stabilizing the RA films and enhancing their resistance to transformation during subsequent cooling. In low-Si steels, the diminished suppression of carbide formation accelerates carbon consumption within martensite, reducing austenite stability and promoting premature bainitic and cementite transformations [ 31 , 36 ].

sections.heading: Tensile results
paragraphs:
The tensile properties of the investigated steels are summarized in  Table 3  and illustrated in  Fig. 17 
                            . At a partitioning temperature of 250 °C ( Fig. 17 (a)), the L-Si steel achieved a YS of approximately 972 MPa and a UTS of ∼1906 MPa, with a TE of 6.8%. In contrast, under the same partitioning conditions, the H-Si steel showed an attractive strength–ductility combination, YS above 1 GPa (∼1046 MPa) and a notably high UTS (2009 MPa, the highest among all tested conditions), along with a greater TE of 8.2% than the L-Si counterparts. This improvement in the H-Si steel can be correlated with its higher RA content: before straining, ∼17 vol% RA vs. ∼14 vol% in L-Si ( Table 3 ). The additional austenite in H-Si likely contributes to a stronger TRIP effect – resulting in enhanced work hardening and sustained plasticity – which explains its higher UTS and elongation.

After the partitioning at 300 °C, the mechanical responses of the two steels diverge more distinctly. The L-Si steel shows an increase in YS to 1213 MPa, but a slight decrease in its UTS to 1638 MPa and TE to 5.3%. The high YS is attributed to a substantial bainite fraction formed at 300 °C, since bainite is a stronger constituent than austenite. This interpretation is supported by Li et al. [ 37 ], who demonstrated that increasing the bainite content in Q&P microstructures raises the material's strength. However, unlike Li et al.’s case where elongation was unaffected by bainite, here the elongation decreased markedly. The key difference is that our 300 °C L-Si microstructure contains almost no retained austenite to compensate for the loss of ductility. It consists predominantly of martensite and ∼23 vol% bainite ( Table 2 ), with only ∼1 vol% RA remaining, essentially a TRIP-less microstructure. Without sufficient RA, there is no significant transformation-induced plasticity to delay necking; consequently, work hardening is reduced and the material fails sooner.

In contrast, the H-Si steel shows a better strength–ductility profile at the same partitioning condition (300 °C, 1000 s). Its YS (∼1042 MPa) remains nearly the same as at 250 °C, slightly lower UTS (∼1823 MPa) while total elongation improves to ∼9.3%. In other words, raising the partitioning temperature to 300 °C in the H-Si steel trades a bit of ultimate strength for a notable gain in ductility. The combination of 1823 MPa UTS and 9.3% elongation is a good balance (PSE ≈16.9 GPa%), comparable to or better than the 250 °C condition (2009 MPa, 8.2%, PSE ≈16.5 GPa%). This improvement stems from the higher RA fraction (∼20 vol% RA before deformation, vs 17 vol% at 250 °C) and its greater stability at 300 °C. Even after tensile deformation, ∼6 vol% RA remained in the H-Si 300 °C sample (compared to ∼3% in 250 °C), confirming that more austenite survived to higher strains. This RA continuously transformed during straining, providing a sustained work-hardening rate ( Fig. 17 (b)) and delaying the onset of necking. Although differences are modest, the H-Si steel partitioned at 300 °C exhibited the highest strain-hardening capacity, correlating with its high uniform elongation.

Regarding the mechanical stability of RA, XRD of strained samples revealed that in this condition (H-Si steel at 300 °C), approximately 14 vol% out of the initial 20 vol% RA transformed to strain-induced martensite during tensile loading (leaving around 6 vol%). Similarly, the H-Si sample partitioned at 250 °C, roughly the same amount of 14 vol% austenite transformed under strain (from 17 to 3 vol%). The higher initial RA in the 300 °C condition simply meant more was left untransformed at fracture. This suggests that the RA in the 300 °C H-Si steel was somewhat more stable, as not all transformed during the tensile deformation. In contrast, the L-Si steel at 250 °C, with ∼14% initial RA, retained only ∼2% after straining (≈12% transformed).

In all cases, the majority of the RA present before deformation transformed to martensite by the end of tensile testing, which is desirable for maximizing the TRIP effect. These observations suggest that the mechanical stability of RA was similar in the high- and low-Si steels for given partitioning conditions, an observation supported also by Ghosh et al. [ 18 ] who reported only marginal differences in RA transformation between 0.25% Si and 1.5% Si Q&P steels.  Table 3  summarizes the mechanical performance of the steels DQ&P processed under the different conditions. The H-Si steel partitioned at 250 °C achieved the highest overall PSE, while the L-Si steel partitioned at 300 °C exhibited the weakest combination of the properties. Such behavior is consistent with its predominantly bainitic-martensitic microstructure containing only a trace of RA; the absence of a significant TRIP contribution leads to early strain localization and premature failure.

The area under the true stress–strain curve is reported in  Table 3 . For the H-Si steel, the total area under the curve at 250 °C was higher overall, but the UE was lower than that observed at 300 °C. Thus, for the high-Si composition, a partitioning temperature of 300 °C yields a superior combination of uniform deformation. The opposite trend was observed in the L-Si steel, where the specimen partitioned at 250 °C exhibited greater UE than the one treated at 300 °C. This contrast is consistent with the microstructural evolution discussed earlier: in the L-Si steel, partitioning at 250 °C effectively stabilized sufficient RA without extensive bainitic transformation, whereas at 300 °C, accelerated bainite formation consumed austenite and degraded ductility. Overall, these results demonstrate that the mechanical behavior of DQ&P steels is governed by the delicate balance between martensitic strength and austenitic stability. High-Si content promotes a sustained TRIP effect by suppressing carbide precipitation and stabilizing carbon-enriched RA, thereby ensuring superior strength–ductility synergy. In contrast, reduced Si levels enhance bainite formation, limiting the extent of RA transformation and compromising the mechanical response.

sections.heading: Post-tensile microstructure (fracture surface)
paragraphs:
The fracture surfaces after tensile testing were analyzed to correlate microscopic failure mechanisms with the observed mechanical behavior. Among the four tested conditions, three samples–H-Si partitioned at 250 °C, H-Si at 300 °C, and L-Si at 250 °C–showed relatively similar fracture response, consistent with their comparable RA fractions. In contrast, L-Si partitioned at 300 °C exhibited distinctly different behavior due to its negligible RA content and substantial bainite formation. Therefore, only the results for H-Si and L-Si at 300 °C are discussed in detail here ( Fig. 18 
                            ).

Fig. 18 (a) shows the fracture surface of the H-Si steel specimen. The surface is dominated by fine and coarse dimples, which are characteristic of ductile fracture through microvoid nucleation, growth, and coalescence. The observed variation in dimple size reflects differences in the density and spatial distribution of void-nucleation sites during plastic deformation. In addition, some local surface discontinuities are visible, consistent with localized damage accumulation prior to final fracture. Overall, the fracture morphology of the H-Si steel indicates a predominantly ductile failure mode with significant plastic deformation, in agreement with its relatively high total elongation.

In contrast, the fracture surface of the L-Si steel partitioned at 300 °C exhibits a markedly different morphology ( Fig. 18 (b)). Pronounced cleavage facets with river patterns are observed, indicating a significant brittle fracture component. Although dimples are still present locally—ranging from isolated larger dimples to finer ones adjacent to cleavage facets—the coexistence of cleavage features and ductile dimples suggests a mixed-mode or quasi-cleavage fracture. Such fracture behavior is commonly associated with high-strength steels in which reduced ductility arises from microstructural hardening and limited transformation-induced plasticity. The very low RA fraction and the high bainite content in the L-Si steel partitioned at 300 °C likely promoted this increased brittle fracture contribution.

Due to the limited spatial resolution of EBSD for detecting very fine, thin and deformed RA as well as extensive post-deformation transformation, EBSD analysis was generally not feasible in most post-tensile specimens. As such, EBSD after tensile testing was conducted only for the H-Si steel partitioned at 300 °C for 1000 s, which retained the highest amount of RA prior to deformation and had the highest and coarser RA before the tensile test ( Fig. 19 
                            ).  Fig. 19 (a), taken approximately 1000 μm from the fracture surface, shows the phase map and image quality (IQ) map. A small fraction of RA is still detectable between martensite laths. However, some regions exhibit lower IQ and darker contrast, indicating that new martensite formed during tensile straining. Moving closer to the fracture surface (∼500 μm),  Fig. 19 (b) reveals further transformation: only trace amounts of RA persist, with the majority having transformed to martensite. This transformation behavior is consistent with earlier studies on Q&P steels, including low-carbon variants [ 38 ], where high strain levels drive extensive strain-induced martensitic transformation.

At this location, most austenite films have been disappeared/transformed, with only a very small amount detectable between laths. Although deformation induced extensive austenite-to-martensite transformation, XRD results indicate that approximately 6 vol% RA persists in this sample, consistent with the RA detected in  Fig. 19 (a and b).

Fig. 19 (c), the view located within the immediate fracture zone, shows a fully martensitic structure, without resolvable RA. Owing to the very fine martensitic microstructure, nano-scale dimensions of some features and the significant plastic deformation imposed, EBSD analysis was quite challenging in this region. However, the captured high quality EBSD-IPF map ( Fig. 19 (d)) clearly showed the crack growth path. It can be seen that fracture propagation occurred preferentially along martensitic lath boundaries and at interfaces between the former RA and the surrounding (tempered) martensitic matrix. The preferential crack propagation along RA/martensite interfaces can be rationalized by the strong local strength/hardness mismatch, which increases strain incompatibility and promotes stress concentrations at phase boundaries. Moreover, strain-induced transformation of RA to martensite imposes additional local transformation strains and may generate fresh, high-carbon martensite with reduced damage tolerance, facilitating interfacial decohesion and crack advance [ 39 ]. These regions are known to be mechanically heterogeneous and may act as stress concentrators during deformation. in addition, there were subtle indications of crack progression along PAG boundaries, although this mode appeared less dominant.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
This study systematically examined the combined effects of two silicon contents (L-Si and H-Si, with 0.25 wt% and 1.5 wt% Si, respectively), two partitioning temperatures, several partitioning durations, and prior deformation on the stabilization of retained austenite (RA) and the mechanical performance of a 0.4C-2Mn-XSi-1Cr-0.02Al-0.49Ni (wt.%) steel processed via the deformation-quenching and partitioning (DQ&P) process. Based on the results obtained, the following conclusions can be drawn: 
                         
                            • 
                            Three-pass deformation (3 × 0.2 strain with 25 s interpass times and 25 s final holding) at 850 °C prior to quenching resulted in complete static recrystallization and effectively refined the prior austenite grain size in both L-Si and H-Si steels. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            Increasing Si from 0.25 to 1.5 wt% suppressed cementite formation during partitioning, enabling higher and more stable RA fractions (typically ∼17–20 vol%) under optimized conditions. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            Deformation partially mitigated the penalty of low Si at 250 °C (raising RA to ∼10–14 vol%) but could not fully compensate for it at 300 °C, where bainite formation consumed nearly all RA in the L-Si steel. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            In the L-Si steel, bainite and carbides developed readily at 300 °C, leaving only minor RA (∼1 vol%). At 250 °C, bainite formation remained limited. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            In the high-Si steel, approximately 20 vol% RA with 0.77% C was obtained after partitioning at 300 °C for 1000 s. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            RA fraction increased with partitioning time up to 1000 s for the H-Si steel at 300 °C and beyond 1000 s for the L-Si steel at 250 °C. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The H-Si steel achieved a UTS of ∼1.8–2.0 GPa with an elongation of ≈8%, owing to sustained TRIP from stabilized RA. The L-Si steel exhibited higher yield strength but reduced elongation after partitioning at 300 °C owing to the bainite formation and minimal RA.
